report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is too absolute. Olive leaf extract *may* modestly lower blood pressure, but evidence is limited and not strong enough to regard it as a proven or guideline-level treatment for hypertension.

A 2011 double-blind randomized trial in people with stage-1 hypertension found 500 mg twice daily lowered systolic and diastolic pressure similarly to captopril. However, it was an *active-comparator* study rather than a placebo-controlled confirmation, so it cannot establish how much of the change was due to the extract itself or whether it prevents cardiovascular events.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/

Evidence is also inconsistent. An 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in overweight/obese adults with mildly raised cholesterol assessed cardiovascular markers, including BP, but does not provide convincing support for a clinically important BP benefit in that broader population.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137474/

A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis evaluated olive-leaf supplementation across cardiovascular outcomes, including BP. Pooling small, varied trials can suggest an average reduction, but differences in extract formulation, oleuropein dose, population, study duration, and study quality mean the estimate remains uncertain—not evidence that any over-the-counter product will work.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y

**Practical interpretation:** It is plausible that olive leaf extract produces a small BP reduction for some people, especially with mild hypertension, but it should not replace clinician-guided treatment, home BP monitoring, DASH-style eating, exercise, weight management, or prescribed medicines. Discuss it with a clinician/pharmacist first—particularly if you use BP or diabetes drugs—because additive BP-lowering could be relevant.
